headline: Marine Parkway After Dark: The Bass Went Nocturnal, So Did I
subhead: With the bay running warm and the bass feeding on their own schedule, I traded daylight boat trips for midnight runs under the bridge.
body_markdown:
I put the boat in at Motts Basin this week instead of launching the kayak off Canarsie Pier, and the reason's simple — the keeper bass in this bay have gone nocturnal on me, and you can't chase a night bite paddling. Once the sun's down and the outgoing starts pulling hard under Marine Parkway Bridge, that's where the grown-up fish are, not stacked up shallow at noon getting sunburned. Shallow water in this bay has been sitting warm for weeks now, and warm shallow water pushes big striped bass onto a low-light clock — they'll slide up under the pilings and hunt the current seams from dusk till the tide slacks, then disappear again with first light. I fished the last two hours of two different outgoing tides this week, one Tuesday and one Friday, and connected on both — a 29-incher on a black Redfin swum slow through the shadow line, and a fat schoolie plus a short bluefish on a bunker chunk soaking on the bottom in about 18 feet. Two trips isn't a trend, but it's the same story I've heard from a couple guys fishing the bridge from small boats — after dark or don't bother if you're after anything over 28 inches right now.

Daytime, I've shifted the whole program to fluke, and that bite has stayed honest while everything else in the bay gets moody. I've been working the channel edges off Ruffle Bar and the flats inside Grassy Bay on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet along bottom in 15 to 22 feet. Nothing enormous — most fish are running 16 to 19 inches with the occasional 20-incher mixed in — but the action's been steady enough that a few drifts will put dinner in the cooler. The Cross Bay Bridge channel has produced too, especially right around the pilings on the bay side where the current funnels bait through, though you need to keep your bucktail tight to structure or you're just fishing empty water. Fluke don't care that the surface is warm — they're sitting on the same bottom structure they always do in July, and moving water is still the whole game.

Out at the inlet, the story's a little rougher than I'd like. The ocean's been kicking up nasty the last several days — close to four-foot swell rolling in off the buoy readings I've seen, short and choppy at five seconds, which is enough to keep me off the jetty rocks at Breezy Point and out of the surf entirely unless it's dead calm at dawn. But that same sloppy ocean is pushing bunker schools tight against the beach, and when the tide's ripping through Rockaway Inlet, blues have been following that bait right into the mouth. I had one afternoon on a strong outgoing where jumbo bluefish showed up chasing bunker pods just inside the inlet, and a guy working topwater poppers off a center console had three fish over 8 pounds in twenty minutes before they moved off with the tide. Inside the bay itself, snapper blues are everywhere off Canarsie Pier right now — great if you've got a kid with a bobber and a piece of spearing, tough if you're trying to set the hook on anything with teeth on light tackle.

Weakfish are the one bright spot I want to flag, because we called this coming — said last week that as the bay kept warming, the weakfish bite would start rebuilding on calm evenings, and that's exactly what's happened. I had a solid hour at Grassy Bay Thursday evening, glass-calm water, working a 3-inch pearl soft plastic on a light jig head slow along the bottom edge of the flat as the tide started to ebb, and picked up four weakfish in the 14 to 17-inch range along with a couple short fluke mixed in. Nothing to call the papers over, but it's a real, repeatable bite on the right evening, and it's building, not fading.

We're coming off the first-quarter moon now, which means the current's easing into a neap cycle — less brutal push through the bridges and the inlet, which should actually widen the productive window at Marine Parkway rather than shrink it, since the bass won't need to sprint the current to stay fed. If the ocean lays down even a little, I'd use that window to check the inlet on the last two hours of an outgoing for blues following bait back out, and I'd keep the fluke program running the flats and channel edges through the softer tides ahead. Best case, the bunker stay tight to the beach and that bluefish pattern keeps pushing into the inlet on the bigger tides. If the swell stays up and keeps things blown out, I'll be back under the bridge after dark with the swimmers, because right now that's still the surest way to touch a real bass in this bay.
